title: With the Samanas

teacherSummary.text: With the Samanas, Siddhartha learns fasting, enduring pain, and meditations that let his self pass into animals and objects. Yet after three years he concludes these are only escapes from the self, not true release. When rumors spread of Gotama, the Buddha, he and Govinda leave; Siddhartha masters the old Samana with his gaze before departing.

With the Samanas the hope is the opposite, “to find tranquility with an emptied heart” (With the Samanas, paragraph 3): empty the container and the “innermost of my being” will appear. A reader could argue that emptying is a real change, because it gives up on teachers; but the Samanas are teachers too, with their own “rules.”

In both chapters the reason is that the guide has not reached the goal: his father, for all his learning, is “just a searching man, a thirsty man?” (The Son of the Brahmin, paragraph 9), and the Samanas, after sixty years, “find comfort, we find numbness, we learn feats” (With the Samanas, paragraph 20). The same reason produces a harder break.

Govinda’s reply is an argument from results, and the chapter’s evidence answers it. Siddhartha calls the exercises “a short numbing of the senses against the pain and the pointlessness of life” (With the Samanas, paragraph 13), the same thing the oxcart driver finds in rice wine. Govinda grants the numbing but denies that the outcome is the same: the drinker will “return from the delusion, finds everything to be unchanged, has not become wiser, has gathered no enlightenment—has not risen several steps” (paragraph 14), which implies that the Samana does rise. That is the right test, a lasting gain, and Siddhartha answers it on Govinda’s own terms. He says that he is “just as far removed from wisdom, from salvation, as a child in the mother’s womb” (paragraph 15), and when Govinda insists that “we have already ascended many a level” (paragraph 17), Siddhartha points to their teacher: “He has lived for sixty years and has not reached the nirvana” (paragraph 20). If sixty years of exercises leave the oldest Samana short of the goal, the rise Govinda claims has not appeared. Siddhartha has the stronger case on the evidence; Govinda’s reply holds only if one trusts a gain that no one around them shows.

The training does not change the object of the thirst; it shows that the thirst outlasts every method. That is why the chapter ends with him leaving again.

items.prompt: Siddhartha leaves his father and the Samanas in very different ways: he waits all night for his father’s consent, but he compels the old Samana with a spell. Does the difference show growth or loss? Argue from both scenes and answer the other reading.
items.author: r11-handwritten
items.expected: The difference reads more as loss than growth. At home he refuses to leave without consent and stands until the father sees that “he had already left him” (The Son of the Brahmin, paragraph 47); his will wins, but by patience, and the blessing is given freely. With the Samanas he “took away his free will, subdued him under his own will” (With the Samanas, paragraph 41) and takes the blessing by force, after whispering that he wants “to show the old man that I’ve learned something from him” (paragraph 40). The man who once waited now commands. The growth reading has a point: the old Samana is angry and abusive, so Siddhartha protects Govinda and leaves with courtesy, and he dismisses the feat at once (“Let old Samanas be content with such feats!”, paragraph 43). But the dismissal comes after he has used it. Both scenes show a will that will not bend, and the second shows what it can do to another person.

segments.script: Asceticism—strict self-denial—was a widespread spiritual practice in ancient India. segments.script: First, meaning. I read “to become empty, empty of thirst, empty of wishing, empty of dreams, empty of joy and sorrow” slowly and put it in my own words: He wants to empty himself of thirst, wishes, dreams, joy and sorrow. What does Siddhartha want from the Samanas' practices? My answer: Siddhartha wants the Samanas' practices to free him from the self, emptying himself through hunger and denial; the story will show this path is not enough to bring him peace.

items.text: What do the Samanas practice?
items.lookFor: Fasting and self-denial
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Fasting, enduring heat, cold and pain, and self-denial meant to empty the self. The goal is stated in “A goal stood before Siddhartha, a single goal: to become empty, empty of thirst, empty of wishing, empty of dreams” (With the Samanas, paragraph 3).

items.text: What can Siddhartha do in meditation?
items.lookFor: Let his self pass into animals and things
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: He can leave his self and pass into other creatures and things. The line is “A heron flew over the bamboo forest—and Siddhartha accepted the heron into his soul” (With the Samanas, paragraph 6).

items.text: What does he conclude about these practices?
items.lookFor: They are only temporary escapes from the self
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: That they are only short escapes from the self, no better than a drunkard’s: “What is meditation? What is leaving one’s body?” (With the Samanas, paragraph 13) and his answer in paragraph 15 that he finds such escapes in himself as the drunkard does in wine.

items.text: Who is rumored to have attained enlightenment?
items.lookFor: Gotama, the Buddha
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Gotama, the Buddha. The rumour is introduced in With the Samanas, paragraph 28 and grows in paragraphs 29–32 (“The myth of Buddha sounded sweet,” paragraph 31).

items.text: How does Siddhartha respond to the old Samana's anger?
items.lookFor: He silences him with his gaze
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: He fixes the old man with his gaze until the Samana falls silent and blesses their leaving: “Positioning himself closely in front of the Samana, with a concentrated soul, he captured the old man’s glance” (With the Samanas, paragraph 41).

items.text: Retell the three most important events of “With the Samanas” in order, in one sentence each.
items.lookFor: With the Samanas, Siddhartha learns fasting, enduring pain, and meditations that let his self pass into animals and objects. Yet after three years he concludes these are only escapes from the self, not true release. When rumors spread of Gotama, the Buddha, he and Govinda leave; Siddhartha masters the old Samana with his gaze before departing.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Siddhartha and Govinda join the Samanas and learn self-denial (With the Samanas, paragraphs 1–7); Siddhartha concludes these are only escapes (paragraphs 11–15, 20); news of Gotama arrives and they leave, Siddhartha overpowering the oldest Samana with his gaze (paragraphs 28, 39–41).

items.text: Which characters appear or are mentioned in “With the Samanas”? Name two and one thing each says or does.
items.lookFor: Names and actions taken from the chapter; check against the teacher summary.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Two of: Govinda, who defends the Samanas’ progress (“We have learned, and we’ll continue learning.” (With the Samanas, paragraph 10)); the oldest Samana, who is angry at their leaving (paragraph 39); the absent Gotama, known only by rumour (paragraph 28).

items.text: Where and when does “With the Samanas” take place? Point to the line that tells you.
items.lookFor: A place/time detail quoted from the chapter.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: In the forest with the Samanas, over about three years. Time: “when the two young men had lived among the Samanas for about three years” (With the Samanas, paragraph 28); place: they beg in the villages from the forest (paragraph 9).

items.text: Reread: “How could you have learned meditation, holding your breath, insensitivity against hunger and pain there among these wretched people?” What does “insensitivity” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?
items.lookFor: insensitivity: lack of feeling; not being affected by something.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Insensitivity” here means: lack of feeling; not being affected by something. In With the Samanas, paragraph 12, Govinda protests that the Samana skills, such as not feeling hunger and pain, could never be learned among drinkers and gamblers.

items.text: Reread: “And the young men returned the bows with thanks, returned the wish, went on their way with salutations.” What does “salutations” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?
items.lookFor: salutations: greetings; polite words or gestures of greeting.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Salutations” here means: greetings; polite words or gestures of greeting. In With the Samanas, paragraph 41, after the old Samana blesses them, the two friends bow, thank him and leave with polite greetings.

items.text: What does “With the Samanas” suggest about self-denial as a path? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: A stated inference (for example, that self-denial can become another way of not finding the self) backed by one located line, such as the one in With the Samanas, paragraph 7.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The chapter suggests self-denial can become another way of not finding the self. Support: “Siddhartha learned a lot when he was with the Samanas, many ways leading away from the self he learned to go.” (With the Samanas, paragraph 7) “away from the self” is the key phrase.

items.text: Find one example of theme in this chapter. What does it reveal that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: Look for statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The theme that discipline escapes rather than finds the self comes through his comparison with the drunkard (With the Samanas, paragraph 15): a plain statement would not show how close his practice is to what he despises.

items.text: How does the characterization in this chapter shape what we understand about self-denial as a path?
items.lookFor: Look for what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Govinda’s steady faith (“We are not going around in circles, we are moving up, the circle is a spiral” (With the Samanas, paragraph 17)) sets off Siddhartha’s doubt and shows that the path’s value depends on the seeker, not the rules.

items.text: In the passage that begins “Many wonderful and unbelievable things were reported of him, he had performed miracles, had overcome the devil, had spoken to the gods.”, why might Hesse have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Diction analysis of two words in the anchor passage.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: In With the Samanas, paragraph 30, “unbelievable” quietly questions the stories even as it repeats them, and “reported” marks them as rumour, not seen fact; the words let the reader feel both the wonder and the doubt that surround the Buddha.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “With the Samanas”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: With the Samanas, Siddhartha learns fasting, enduring pain, and meditations that let his self pass into animals and objects. Yet after three years he concludes these are only escapes from the self, not true release. When rumors spread of Gotama, the Buddha, he and Govinda leave; Siddhartha masters…
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The turn is his conclusion that the Samanas’ way leads nowhere (paragraphs 20–22), brought to a head by the Buddha rumour (paragraph 28). Effect: he and Govinda leave to hear Gotama in the next chapter.

items.text: How does “With the Samanas” build on “The Son of the Brahmin”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal or structural link between this and the previous chapter.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Cause and effect: the discontent of “The Son of the Brahmin” (paragraph 8) sends him to the Samanas, whose path he now finds empty too, so the search moves on again. Link line: “Siddhartha gave his garments to a poor Brahmin in the street.” (With the Samanas, paragraph 2)

items.text: What can we infer about a character's motives from what they say and do here, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: An inference about motive supported by a quoted line.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Siddhartha claims to want learning, but his mockery of the oldest Samana (paragraph 20) shows he already wants out; Govinda claims progress but is moved by loyalty and hope (“Your willingness delights my heart.” (With the Samanas, paragraph 37)).

items.text: The bell-ringer asked: “Siddhartha calls the Samanas' practices a 'brief numbing.' Do you agree?” Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer anchored in the text.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A revised answer should use his own words, “a short numbing of the senses” (With the Samanas, paragraph 13), and test them against paragraph 6, where his escapes into heron and jackal always end: he “awoke every time to find his old self again.”

items.text: Where does imagery appear, and how does it connect this chapter to the larger concern with experience versus teaching?
items.lookFor: Look for sensory details (sight, sound, cold, light) and what mood they create.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The heron and the decaying jackal (With the Samanas, paragraph 6) are vivid sensory images of leaving the self; they connect to the larger concern because they are experiences given by a teacher’s method, and each ends where it began.

items.text: Background: Asceticism—strict self-denial—was a widespread spiritual practice in ancient India. How does knowing this change the way you read one moment in the chapter?
items.lookFor: A specific moment reread in light of the context.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Knowing asceticism was common and respected shows that Siddhartha’s doubt is radical: he questions a whole culture’s path, not a fad, as when he says the oldest Samana has not reached nirvana in sixty years (With the Samanas, paragraph 20).

items.text: A critic might argue: “Siddhartha discovers that discipline alone can become another form of illusion, a key turn in his quest.” How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the chapter.
items.lookFor: A defended position with evidence and one counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Agree: paragraph 7 says the ways he learned lead “away from the self” and paragraph 6 shows every escape returning to the old self. A counterpoint from the text is Govinda’s spiral (With the Samanas, paragraph 17), the view that slow progress is still progress.

items.text: Which character in this chapter acts most wisely, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: An evaluation using an explicit criterion and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Siddhartha acts most wisely if the standard is honesty about results (paragraph 20); the oldest Samana least, because he reacts with anger, not reasons (paragraph 39). Some will judge Govinda wisest for humility (paragraph 21).

items.text: Rewrite one moment of “With the Samanas” from the point of view of a different character. What does the new angle reveal or hide about self-denial as a path?
items.lookFor: A rewrite that keeps the chapter’s events accurate, speaks in the chosen character’s voice, and ends with a sentence on what the new angle shows or hides.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Govinda’s view of the parting from the old Samana (With the Samanas, paragraphs 39–41) is a good choice: from his angle the gaze looks like magic (paragraph 42), which hides Siddhartha’s own doubts.

items.text: Write three questions of your own about “With the Samanas”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions at three levels, each answerable from the chapter, traded and answered with a line.
followUps: Which of your three questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Example set: recall, ‘How long do they stay with the Samanas?’ (about three years, paragraph 28); why/how, ‘Why does Siddhartha doubt the Samanas?’ (paragraph 20); what if, ‘Should Govinda have stayed?’

items.text: Connect this chapter to the unity of all things: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Hesse need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment of thematic development across the work.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Only a hint so far: in meditation he becomes heron, jackal, stone and water (With the Samanas, paragraph 6), a first taste of oneness that is still escape, not insight. Hesse would need to show oneness found without leaving the self.

items.text: Is the theme in this chapter effective, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: An evaluative judgment with criteria and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Effective because the theme is argued in dialogue (paragraphs 9–15, 17–23), not announced; it can feel heavy where Siddhartha’s conclusions are stated outright, as in paragraph 15.

items.text: Compare how “With the Samanas” treats self-denial as a path with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Siddhartha see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A cross-text synthesis.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A comparison should name a parallel discipline (extreme training or diet, a strict program) and quote paragraph 7’s “away from the self” to show Siddhartha’s particular objection: the discipline works, but it is escape.

items.text: Predict what “Gotama” will bring, using two clues from this chapter. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction or judgment justified with textual clues.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Clues: the Buddha rumour (“The myth of Buddha sounded sweet.” (With the Samanas, paragraph 31)) and Siddhartha’s doubt that any teaching can give what he seeks (paragraph 22). Prediction: they meet Gotama, and Siddhartha may again stand apart.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of this chapter (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about self-denial as a path?
items.lookFor: A modern setting, characters and conflict that keep the chapter’s core idea, with the one element that must not change named.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: A modern version keeps a seeker who masters a hard discipline and finds it leaves the self unchanged. What must stay is the moment of honest doubt, as in paragraph 20.

items.text: What question would you most like to ask Hermann Hesse about this chapter, and what answer do you think the text itself gives?
items.lookFor: A student-generated question answered from evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Example: ‘Did Siddhartha waste three years?’ The text answers no and yes: he learned real skills (With the Samanas, paragraph 42) but found them “leading away from the self” (paragraph 7).

contentNotes.teacherNote: Among the worldly sights Siddhartha rejects are “whores offering themselves” (Hesse, 1922/2015, With the Samanas, para. 2), and he speaks of “In every tavern of that part of a town where the whorehouses are, my friend, among carters and gamblers I could have learned it.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, With the Samanas, para. 11). These are dated, derogatory words for sex workers and brothels (places where sex is sold); today say “sex workers” or “brothel.” They show his contempt for city life. The chapter also shows ascetic self-punishment, framed as religious practice that the novel judges a dead end: “It is fleeing from the self, it is a short escape of the agony of being a self, it is a short numbing of the senses against the pain and the pointlessness of life.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, With the Samanas, para. 13)
